div.head: About the eLiebermann Project
div.p: The eLiebermann database is a digital research platform for the laws and legal language of early England. Its foundation is Felix Liebermann's Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen (1903–16), still the standard complete edition of the early English laws, which it makes searchable, interlinked and accessible to Anglophone readers. Around that core it collates later editions, translations and scholarship, so that the text of a law, the words it uses, and what scholars have said about both can be studied in one place.
The platform has three parts:

The project grows out of research on the language and composition of the earliest English law codes. Its aims are to open Liebermann's foundational work to more scholars, and to facilitate new research into the earliest English written laws.
At present eLiebermann holds:

list.item: 9,246 dictionary entries, the whole of the Wörterbuch;
2,547 clauses from 78 law codes and legal texts, from the laws of Æthelberht of Kent to those of William I and Henry I;
the texts and translations of a number of more modern editions, among them those of F. L. Attenborough and A. J. Robertson;
1,348 cross-references between clauses from Liebermann's apparatus, and about 1,500 more from later scholars, each linked in both directions.

div.p: eLiebermann is a work in progress. New material is added, and existing material corrected, continuously. The principles on which the texts have been edited, and the methods by which they have been transcribed, checked and encoded, are set out under Editorial Principles.

div.head: Felix Liebermann and Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen
div.p: Felix Liebermann (born Berlin, 20 July 1851; died Berlin, 7 October 1925) was a German historian of medieval England, and the foremost authority of his generation on Anglo-Saxon and Anglo-Norman law. He came from a prosperous Jewish family in Berlin; the painter Max Liebermann was his elder brother. He began in business, in banking and the textile trade, and it was while he was living in Manchester that he became interested in English history. In 1873 he went to Göttingen to study it under Georg Waitz and Reinhold Pauli, and took his doctorate in 1875 with a study of the Dialogus de Scaccario. From 1877 to 1885 he worked as an editor for the Monumenta Germaniae Historica, for which he edited extracts from thirteenth-century English historians.

Liebermann held no regular university post, and spent the rest of his life as an independent scholar in Berlin. In a long series of studies he edited and explained the legal compilations of the early twelfth century through which most of the Old English laws were transmitted: the Quadripartitus (1892), the Consiliatio Cnuti (1893), the Leges Edwardi Confessoris (1896) and the Leges Henrici (1901). The universities of Oxford and Cambridge gave him honorary degrees in 1896. His English lecture The National Assembly in the Anglo-Saxon Period appeared in 1913.
His great work, Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen, was published in Halle for the Savigny-Stiftung, in three volumes and four parts:

list.item: I. Text und Übersetzung (1903): the texts of all the laws, from Æthelberht to the Anglo-Norman compilations, with the readings of every manuscript printed in parallel columns, a German translation, and marginal cross-references between clauses;
II.1. Wörterbuch (1906): a dictionary of every word in the laws;
II.2. Rechts- und Sachglossar (1912): a glossary of legal and historical subjects;
III. Einleitung zu jedem Stück; Erklärungen zu einzelnen Stellen (1916): an introduction to each text and a commentary on individual passages.

div.p: More than a century later the Gesetze remains the edition from which the laws are commonly cited, and much of what has been written on early English law since rests on it. But it is not an easy book to use. It is written in a heavily abbreviated academic German, it depends on hundreds of sigla, and its apparatus is dense and occasionally inconsistent. Parts of its scholarship have also been substantially revised by later studies. eLiebermann keeps Liebermann's text as he printed it, and sets beside it the work of the century since.

div.head: Citing eLiebermann
div.p: When you use eLiebermann, you can open the linked archive.org pdfs of Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen to confirm the text and cite directly to the printed work:
Felix Liebermann, ed. and trans., Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen, 3 vols (Halle: Niemeyer, 1903–16).
If you would like to cite directly to the eLiebermann database, you can use this form:

A dictionary entry: “bocland”, eLiebermann Legal Dictionary, ed. Anya Adair, https://anyaadair.github.io/eLiebermann/entry.html?id=bocland (accessed 15 October 2026); after Felix Liebermann, ed. and trans., Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen, 3 vols (Halle: Niemeyer, 1903–16), II.1, p. 26.

A law-code clause: “Ine 23.2”, eLiebermann Lawcodes Database, ed. Anya Adair, https://anyaadair.github.io/eLiebermann/law.html?id=Ine_23-2 (accessed 15 October 2026); after Felix Liebermann, ed. and trans., Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen, 3 vols (Halle: Niemeyer, 1903–16), I, p. 98.
When quoting a modern edition or translation of a clause, please cite that edition as well; its full reference is given on the page.

div.head: Funding
div.p: The work described here was supported by a grant from the Research Grants Council of Hong Kong (General Research Fund, Project No. HKU 17604022), for the project The Language and Style of the Earliest English Law Codes (PI: Anya Adair).

div.head: Code and data
div.p: The site's code and all its data are on GitHub at github.com/anyaadair/eLiebermann: the dictionary entries and clauses as TEI XML, the authority lists of law codes, manuscripts and abbreviations, the scripts that build the site, and the reports of collation and checking.
Liebermann's text and translation are in the public domain.
